Bring the rental agreement, the 31-day accounting (or proof none arrived), the Portland Condition Report if applicable, and dated move-in and move-out photos.

faqs.question: What can a landlord deduct from a deposit in Pennsylvania?

faqs.question: Where does my deposit have to be kept in Tennessee?
faqs.answer: In an account used only for security deposits at a bank or lending institution regulated by the state or federal government, and you must be told the account's location when you sign the lease. A landlord who skips this and also fails to provide the required damage listing is not entitled to keep any part of your deposit — regardless of damage.

faqs.question: Can I attend the move-out inspection in Tennessee?
faqs.answer: Yes, and you should. The landlord may notify you of the right when asking you to vacate or within 5 days of your written notice; the inspection happens on move-out day or within 4 calendar days after. Together you compile a listing of damage with estimated repair costs, and both sign it — the signed list is conclusive evidence of what the unit looked like. Disagree? State each disputed item in writing. Skip the inspection with waiver language in your lease and you may lose the right to contest the damages at all.

faqs.question: What can a landlord deduct from a deposit in Tennessee?
faqs.answer: Unpaid rent or other amounts owed under the lease, physical damage identified on the inspection listing (or discovered within the 30-day/7-day window), and contractual damages the lease provides for. Ordinary wear and tear isn't damage.

faqs.question: What if the landlord never gave me a damage listing?
faqs.answer: In URLTA counties, a landlord who failed to keep the deposit in a proper account and failed to provide the damage listing may not retain any portion of the deposit. That forfeiture — not a doubling — is Tennessee's penalty.

faqs.question: Where do deposit disputes go in Tennessee?
faqs.answer: General Sessions Court, Tennessee's small-claims-style court, hears civil claims up to $25,000 ($15,000 in Anderson, Davidson, Hamilton, and Knox counties). Bring the lease, the account disclosure, the signed inspection listing or your written dissent, the refund notice and your response, and dated move-in and move-out photos.

faqs.question: How long does a landlord have to return a security deposit in Texas?
faqs.answer: 30 days after you surrender the premises. The refund goes to your forwarding address, so give that address to the landlord in writing — the landlord's refund and itemization duties are conditioned on it, though you never lose the deposit itself by forgetting to provide one. Miss the deadline, and the law presumes the landlord acted in bad faith.

faqs.question: Is there a limit on security deposits in Texas?
faqs.answer: No. Texas sets no cap on deposit amounts — landlords may charge what the market bears. That makes Texas one of the higher-stakes deposit states in practice: with no ceiling on the deposit, there's no ceiling on what a move-out disagreement is worth.

faqs.question: Can a Texas landlord charge a fee instead of a security deposit?
faqs.answer: Yes, but only as an option under § 92.111. The landlord must also offer the security-deposit option, cannot use your choice to approve or reject your application, and must give written notice of both options, their charges, and your right to switch to the deposit at any time. The fee agreement must be written and signed by both sides. A fee does not erase your duty to pay rent or legally chargeable damage beyond normal wear and tear.

faqs.question: What is the penalty for wrongfully keeping a deposit in Texas?
faqs.answer: A landlord who retains a deposit in bad faith owes $100 plus three times the portion wrongfully withheld plus the tenant's reasonable attorney's fees. And the presumption works in the tenant's favor: if the landlord missed the 30-day deadline, bad faith is presumed unless the landlord can rebut it.

faqs.question: Does my landlord have to itemize deductions in Texas?
faqs.answer: Yes — if any portion is kept, the landlord must provide the balance, if any, with a written description and itemized list of all deductions. The narrow statutory exception is when the tenant owes rent at surrender and there is no controversy about the amount owed. A landlord who in bad faith skips the itemization forfeits the right to withhold anything and the right to sue for the damage, and owes the tenant's reasonable attorney's fees.

faqs.question: Can a Texas landlord charge for normal wear and tear?
faqs.answer: No. Deterioration from ordinary, intended use of the unit — worn carpet paths, faded paint, minor scuffs — cannot be deducted. The line is crossed only by damage from negligence, carelessness, accident, or abuse. In an action brought by a tenant under the security-deposit subchapter, it's the landlord's burden to prove that retaining each portion was reasonable.

faqs.question: Does Texas require a move-in inspection or checklist?
faqs.answer: No — Texas mandates no checklist, condition report, or photos at any point. That cuts both ways: nothing forces documentation, and nothing protects the party who skipped it. Because the landlord bears the burden of proving deductions and the tenant benefits from the bad-faith presumption, a dated room-by-room record made at move-in and move-out is what each side wishes it had when the itemization gets disputed.

faqs.question: Do I have to give notice before moving out to get my deposit back?
faqs.answer: Only if your lease says so — and Texas law makes such a clause effective only when the requirement is underlined or printed in conspicuous bold print in the lease. A buried advance-notice condition generally can't cost you the deposit. Check your lease's surrender language before you plan the move.

faqs.question: Where do deposit disputes go in Texas?
faqs.answer: Justice court — Texas's small claims venue — which handles claims up to $20,000, more than enough to cover treble damages on almost any residential deposit. The process is informal and built for people without lawyers, and the attorney's-fee provision in the deposit statute means a tenant with a strong case can often find counsel worth the claim.

faqs.question: How long does a landlord have to return a security deposit in Utah?
faqs.answer: 30 days after you vacate and return possession. Within that window the landlord must mail or deliver, or send electronically if you authorized it, the balance of your deposit and any prepaid rent, with a written notice itemizing and explaining every deduction.

faqs.question: How much can a landlord charge for a security deposit in Utah?
faqs.answer: There's no statutory cap, no interest requirement, and no rule on where the money is kept. What Utah requires is disclosure: any part of the deposit that will be nonrefundable must be stated in writing when you pay it.

faqs.question: Can a Utah landlord keep a 'nonrefundable' deposit?
faqs.answer: Only if it was disclosed in writing as nonrefundable at the time it was collected (§ 57-17-2). A fee that was never labeled nonrefundable in writing is treated as a refundable deposit.

faqs.question: What can a landlord deduct from a deposit in Utah?
faqs.answer: Unpaid rent, damage you caused beyond normal wear and tear, cleaning, and other costs your lease specifically provides for — each itemized and explained in the written notice. Ordinary aging of paint, carpet, and fixtures isn't deductible.

faqs.question: My landlord missed the 30 days. What do I do?
faqs.answer: Serve the landlord with a written notice — the Utah Courts publish the form, Tenant's Notice to Provide Deposit Disposition. The landlord then has 5 business days to return the deposit and prepaid rent balance with the itemized notice. If they don't, you can sue for the full deposit, all prepaid rent, and a $100 penalty.

faqs.question: Can I recover attorney fees in Utah?
faqs.answer: Only if you had to sue and the court finds the landlord acted in bad faith — then court costs and attorney fees are added to the full deposit, prepaid rent, and $100 penalty. Utah has no double or treble damages.

faqs.question: Does Utah require a move-in inspection or photos?
faqs.answer: No. The chapter has no checklist, walkthrough, or photo requirement. That leaves normal wear and tear to the evidence — and in a dispute over what the unit looked like on day one, the side with dated room-by-room documentation usually wins.

faqs.question: Where do deposit disputes go in Utah?
faqs.answer: Small claims court, in justice court or district court, handles claims up to $20,000 through 2029 — informal and inexpensive. Bring the lease, your written nonrefundable disclosure if any, the Tenant's Notice with proof of service, the itemized notice or proof none arrived, and dated move-in and move-out photos.

faqs.question: How long does a landlord have to return a security deposit in Virginia?
faqs.answer: 45 days after the tenancy ends or you move out, whichever is later. The landlord must return the deposit along with a written, itemized statement of any deductions.

faqs.question: How much can a landlord charge for a security deposit in Virginia?
faqs.answer: No more than two months' periodic rent — in money or 'value,' so pet deposits and other security-type charges count toward the same two-month cap.

faqs.question: What is Virginia's move-in inspection report?
faqs.answer: Within 5 days after you take occupancy, the landlord must give you a written report itemizing damage that already exists. Read it carefully: it's deemed correct unless you object in writing within 5 days. Your objection — ideally with dated photos — becomes the baseline for the whole tenancy.

faqs.question: Can I be present at the move-out inspection in Virginia?
faqs.answer: Yes. The landlord must notify you in writing of your right to be present. If you request it in writing, the landlord tells you the date and time, and the inspection happens within 72 hours of when you hand back possession. Afterward you get a written disposition statement with an itemized list of any damage claimed.

faqs.question: What can a landlord deduct from a deposit in Virginia?
faqs.answer: Accrued rent and reasonable late charges, damage from your noncompliance with the lease (minus reasonable wear and tear), other charges the rental agreement provides for, and actual damages for breach. Ordinary aging of paint, carpet, and fixtures isn't deductible.

faqs.question: What happens if the landlord willfully breaks these rules?
faqs.answer: The court must order return of the deposit plus your actual damages and reasonable attorney's fees. Virginia doesn't double or triple the deposit — but the fee award means a lawyer can be worth hiring in a clear-cut case outside the Small Claims Division.

faqs.question: Does my deposit earn interest in Virginia?
faqs.answer: No. Virginia repealed its deposit-interest requirement; the current statute contains no interest obligation.

faqs.question: Where do deposit disputes go in Virginia?
faqs.answer: The General District Court's Small Claims Division handles claims up to $5,000 — and Virginia bars attorneys from that division for both sides, so it's a true do-it-yourself forum. Bring the lease, the move-in damage report and your written objection, the move-out disposition statement, and dated move-in and move-out photos.

faqs.question: How long does a landlord have to return a security deposit in Vermont?
faqs.answer: 14 days from the date you vacated — if you told the landlord that date — or from the date the landlord discovers you've left. Within that window the landlord must return the deposit with a written statement itemizing any deductions, hand-delivered or mailed to your last known address. Seasonal rentals that aren't a primary residence get 60 days. Give your move-out date and forwarding address in writing.

faqs.question: How much can a landlord charge for a security deposit in Vermont?
faqs.answer: There's no statewide cap and no statewide interest requirement. Municipalities may add local rules, including rules about interest, so check the ordinance where the unit sits. Note the broad definition: any refundable advance, deposit, or prepaid rent, however named, is a security deposit.

faqs.question: What can a landlord deduct from a deposit in Vermont?
faqs.answer: Exactly four things: unpaid rent; damage to the landlord's property that isn't normal wear and tear or the result of events beyond your control; unpaid utility or other charges you owed directly; and the cost of removing belongings you abandoned. faqs.question: What happens if the landlord misses the 14 days?
faqs.answer: The landlord forfeits the right to withhold any portion of the deposit — the whole amount comes back regardless of damage. And if the failure was willful, the landlord owes double the amount wrongfully withheld plus your reasonable attorney's fees and costs.

faqs.question: What if damage happened because of something outside my control?
faqs.answer: Vermont is one of the few states that says so explicitly: damage resulting from actions or events beyond the tenant's control can't be deducted. A burst pipe, a storm, a break-in — not your deposit's problem.

faqs.question: What if the building is sold?
faqs.answer: The deposit transfers to the new landlord, who must give you actual notice of their name and address and confirm that your deposit was transferred. Keep that notice — it tells you who owes the refund.

faqs.question: Does Vermont require a move-in inspection or photos?
faqs.answer: No. The statute has no checklist, walkthrough, or photo requirement. That leaves 'normal wear and tear' — and 'events beyond the tenant's control' — to the evidence, and the side with dated room-by-room documentation from move-in usually wins.

faqs.question: Where do deposit disputes go in Vermont?

faqs.question: How long does a landlord have to return a security deposit in Washington?
faqs.answer: 30 days after the tenancy ends and the tenant vacates. Within that window the landlord must deliver a full and specific statement of any amount retained, documentation supporting the deductions, and the refund. The old 21-day deadline was replaced on July 23, 2023 — if a source says 21 days, it's out of date.

faqs.question: Can a landlord collect a deposit without a move-in checklist in Washington?
faqs.answer: No. RCW 59.18.260 makes a written, signed condition checklist a precondition to collecting any deposit at all. The checklist must describe the condition and cleanliness of the premises, fixtures, equipment, appliances, and furnishings; both landlord and tenant sign and date it, and the tenant gets a copy. A landlord who takes a deposit without one is liable for the full deposit, plus the tenant's costs and attorney's fees.

faqs.question: What can a landlord deduct from a deposit in Washington?
faqs.answer: Damage beyond wear resulting from ordinary use, and unpaid rent or other amounts owed — with hard limits added in 2023. A landlord cannot withhold anything for ordinary-use wear, cannot charge for carpet cleaning without documenting wear beyond ordinary use, cannot deduct for repairing or replacing items whose condition wasn't reasonably documented on the move-in checklist, and cannot charge more than the cost of fixing the damaged portion when the whole item isn't ruined.

faqs.question: Does my Washington landlord have to prove deductions with receipts?
faqs.answer: For tenancies that began on or after July 23, 2023, yes — the retention statement must come with copies of estimates, invoices, or receipts supporting each deduction. A bare list of charges no longer satisfies the statute.

faqs.question: What happens if the landlord misses the 30-day deadline?
faqs.answer: The landlord becomes liable for the full deposit and is barred from asserting any claim to keep any of it. If the refusal was intentional, the court may award up to twice the deposit. In any suit over the deposit, the prevailing party also recovers costs and reasonable attorney's fees — which raises the stakes of guessing wrong for both sides.

faqs.question: Is there a limit on security deposit amounts in Washington?
faqs.answer: No statewide cap. However, nonrefundable fees must be clearly labeled as fees rather than deposits, and some cities layer on local rules — Seattle, for example, restricts deposit amounts and allows installment payments under municipal law. Check your city's code.

faqs.question: Where does my landlord have to keep my deposit?
faqs.answer: In a trust account at a Washington financial institution or with a licensed escrow agent, and you're entitled to a written receipt naming the depository. No interest is owed on the deposit, but failing to provide the receipt is its own compliance violation.

faqs.question: Can my landlord charge me for repainting or new carpet after I move out?
faqs.answer: Only for damage beyond wear resulting from ordinary use — and only in proportion. Faded paint and traffic-worn carpet are ordinary use and can't be charged at all. Carpet cleaning requires documented wear beyond ordinary use. And if you damaged one section of a carpet or wall, the landlord can charge to fix that portion, not to replace the whole thing.

faqs.question: How much can a landlord charge for a security deposit in Wisconsin?

faqs.question: Can my landlord charge me for carpet cleaning in Wisconsin?

faqs.answer: There's no statutory cap, no interest requirement, and no rule on where the money is kept. The article covers only refundable deposits — a fee labeled nonrefundable up front isn't a security deposit under the definition.

faqs.question: What can a landlord deduct from a deposit in West Virginia?
faqs.answer: Five categories: unpaid rent and late fees under the lease; damage from your noncompliance, less reasonable wear and tear; unpaid utilities the landlord was billed for and paid; reasonable costs of removing and storing belongings you left behind; and other charges the rental agreement specifically provides for, including contractor services. Ordinary aging of paint and carpet is reasonable wear.

faqs.question: What is the 15-day extension?
faqs.answer: If the damage exceeds your deposit and needs a third-party contractor, the landlord can send you written notice within the normal notice period and then take an additional 15 days to deliver the itemization and repair costs. The extension only applies when the landlord gave that timely notice.

faqs.question: What happens if the landlord willfully keeps money or ignores the deadline?
faqs.answer: If the noncompliance is willful or not in good faith, you're entitled to judgment for the unreturned deposit plus damages for annoyance and inconvenience equal to one and a half times the amount wrongfully withheld. If you owe rent, the court credits the award against it. The section doesn't add attorney's fees.

faqs.question: How does the landlord have to deliver the deposit and itemization?
faqs.answer: In person, or by mail to your last known address or the forwarding address you provided. Give a forwarding address in writing on move-out day so the mailing reaches you rather than the unit you just left.

faqs.question: Does West Virginia require a move-in inspection or photos?
faqs.answer: No. The article has no checklist, walkthrough, or photo requirement. That leaves 'reasonable wear and tear' to the evidence — and in a magistrate court dispute, the side with dated room-by-room documentation from move-in usually wins.

faqs.question: Where do deposit disputes go in West Virginia?
faqs.answer: Magistrate court — or circuit court — in the county where the property sits, as § 37-6A-5 specifies; magistrate court hears civil claims up to $20,000. Bring the lease, your forwarding address, the itemization or proof none arrived within the notice period, and dated move-in and move-out photos.

faqs.question: How long does a landlord have to return a security deposit in Wyoming?
faqs.answer: 30 days after the rental agreement ends, or 15 days after the landlord receives your new mailing address — whichever is later. If the landlord is claiming damage to the unit, that period is extended by 30 days. Within the window you get the balance of the deposit and any prepaid rent, without interest, plus a written itemization of deductions and the reasons. Send your new address in writing when you leave.

faqs.question: How much can a landlord charge for a security deposit in Wyoming?
faqs.answer: There's no statutory cap, and the statute says the refund is made without interest. What Wyoming regulates is disclosure: if any part of the deposit is nonrefundable, the lease must say so and you must get separate written notice when you pay it.

faqs.question: Can a Wyoming landlord keep a 'nonrefundable' deposit?
faqs.answer: Only if it was disclosed twice: the rental agreement must state that the portion is nonrefundable, and the landlord must give you written notice of that when the deposit is taken (§ 1-21-1207). A fee that shows up as 'nonrefundable' for the first time at move-out is a refundable deposit.

faqs.question: What can a landlord deduct from a deposit in Wyoming?
faqs.answer: Accrued rent, damage beyond reasonable wear and tear, the cost to clean the unit back to its condition at the start of the lease, and other costs your contract provides for — each itemized with reasons in the written statement. Ordinary aging of paint and carpet isn't deductible.

faqs.question: What happens if the landlord unreasonably ignores the deadline or the itemization?
faqs.answer: You may recover the full deposit plus court costs — the statute's word is 'unreasonably fails to comply.' Wyoming has no double or treble damages and no attorney's fee award, so most tenants bring it in small claims without a lawyer.

faqs.question: How are utility deposits handled in Wyoming?
faqs.answer: Separately. A utilities deposit must be refunded within 10 days after you show all utility charges are paid; if you don't show that within 45 days, the landlord may apply it to any unpaid utility debt within 15 days and return the surplus within 7 days (or 15 days after your new address), whichever is later.

faqs.question: Does Wyoming require a move-in inspection or photos?
faqs.answer: No. Article 12 has no checklist, walkthrough, or photo requirement. That leaves 'condition at the beginning of the rental agreement' entirely to the evidence — and in a small claims dispute, the side with dated room-by-room documentation from move-in usually wins.

faqs.question: Where do deposit disputes go in Wyoming?
faqs.answer: The Small Claims Division of the Circuit Court, for claims up to $6,000 — informal, and attorneys are optional. Bring the lease, any nonrefundable-fee disclosure, your new-address notice, the itemization or proof none arrived, and dated move-in and move-out photos.
